Roots of Unity Lattice

Complex AnalysisUnit Distance ProblemNumber Theory
Game: Build a cloud of points from a few unit-length arrows, then see how many pairs end up exactly one step apart, compared with a plain square grid of the same size.
How to play: Choose how many directions the arrows can point (m) and how many of each you may use (r). Tap a dot to see its neighbours.

Look for the math

Let z = e2πi/m be a step of 1/m of a full turn. Every power of z is a unit-length arrow. If you add up whole-number multiples of the arrows 1, z, z², …, you get points of the plane. Two points that differ by one arrow are exactly 1 apart.

A grid with more dimensions

The number of arrows you need before the rest are combinations of them is φ(m): 4 for m = 5, 8 or 12, and 6 for m = 7 or 9. Using each of those arrows 0 to r times gives (r + 1)φ(m) points, a four- or six-dimensional grid flattened onto the plane. The test checks that no two of them land on top of each other, so nothing is lost.

More neighbours per point

A point inside has up to m (or 2m, for odd m) neighbours, one for each arrow and its opposite. A square grid at the best spacing for c² = 25 has 12. The test confirms that the pairs it counts by looking for arrows are exactly the pairs at distance 1, for every shape offered here.

Who wins?

Neither, always. For 81 points with m = 12 the flattened grid has 288 unit pairs against 224 for the best square grid, and for 256 points 1,056 against 976. But with 625 points the square grid is ahead again (3,144 against 2,800), because the edge of the box in four dimensions loses neighbours. This is a toy of an idea, not a proof of anything: the real power of the idea only shows for huge n.

Where this connects

In 2026 an OpenAI model disproved Erdős's conjecture with a construction of this general kind: a grid in a high-dimensional space built from algebraic integers, projected into the plane. The article describes it in these terms and gives no formula. Roots of unity are the simplest algebraic integers of absolute value 1, which is why they make a good toy. The actual construction is far more careful about which number system it uses.

Try m = 12 with r from 1 to 5. At which sizes does the lattice beat the grid, and what changes as r grows?
